title: A Visitor for the Cellar Anew
premise: Elodie Villalobos, a meticulous property surveyor, is hired to appraise Hollowmere House before its demolition, and quickly realizes the house responds to being measured—rooms shift, doors multiply, and the cellar holds a door sealed from the inside. As an excavation crew unearths it, Elodie learns the house was built over a vanished family whose neighbors sang them into silence, and that the song's final verse, never sung aloud, is the only thing keeping them buried. To finish the appraisal honestly, Elodie must recover the verse from the memories the house keeps, resisting its pull to join the chorus himself. In the end he sings the last verse alone in the cellar, freeing the family at the cost of his own name from every record—the house finally appraised at nothing, and demolished.
about_author: Beatrix Fairweather is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent fifteen years cataloguing condemned properties across the American Midwest. She writes horror about structures that remember what people prefer to forget.

chapters.title: The Square Footage of Silence
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Arriving at Hollowmere House to conduct a pre-demolition appraisal, Elodie finds his measurements won't reconcile: the hallway is four feet longer on his second pass. He notes it professionally, keeps the lights on, counts eleven doors where blueprints show ten. The beat is quiet unease masked by professional detachment.

chapters.title: Eleven Doors, Ten Rooms
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. He maps the house room by room, discovering the eleventh door leads nowhere—a wall that wasn't there yesterday. At night he hears humming through the floorboards, a tune he almost knows. The emotional beat: his instinct to document warring with his instinct to flee.

chapters.title: What the Excavator Found
chapters.summary: POV crew foreman Marcus Hale. The excavation crew unearths a stone doorway beneath the cellar floor, sealed from the inside with mortar and, impossibly, furniture. Marcus dismisses the workers' fear; Elodie recognizes the humming is louder now, coming up through the ground. Beat: dread becomes shared, undeniable.

chapters.title: The Appraisal That Appraises Back
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. The house begins reflecting him: rooms rearranged to mirror his childhood home, photographs of a family he doesn't recognize wearing his grandmother's face. He researches county records and finds the Aldous family, vanished in 1911, their neighbors' testimony suspiciously identical. Beat: the personal intrudes; invisibility fails.

chapters.title: A Song in Three Verses
chapters.summary: POV elderly neighbor Ruth Okonkwo, who grew up near Hollowmere. She reveals the town sang a 'rounding song' to shame the Aldouses out—two verses recorded, a third never sung, its words deliberately lost. Whoever completes the song opens the door. Beat: exposition as confession; guilt inherited.

chapters.title: Sealed from the Inside
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Breaking into county archives, he learns the Aldouses didn't vanish—they were driven into the cellar and the door mortared shut while the town sang above. The house has been holding the memory ever since, offering it to anyone who measures honestly. Beat: horror reframed as injustice; loyalty to truth over town.

chapters.title: Join the Chorus
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. The house turns coercive: the song plays in his head constantly, his own voice harmonizing without permission. Marcus, half-claimed already, begs him to sing and be done with it. Elodie nearly does—feeling how good it would feel to belong. Beat: temptation at its peak; loyalty vs. self-preservation.

chapters.title: The Verse Nobody Wrote Down
chapters.summary: POV Ruth. Dying and lucid, she gives Elodie the third verse—not words she memorized but words her mother refused to sing, kept only as rhythm. The house, listening, goes still for the first time. Beat: fragile hope; the passing of witness from one keeper to another.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. As demolition begins early, Elodie descends alone and sings the completed song at the sealed door. It opens onto not bones but the family, waiting, whole in the house's memory. They ask him to stay and keep singing. Beat: climax—compassion against annihilation, justice outside any law.

chapters.title: Appraised at Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Marcus. The house comes down cleanly; records list no surveyor named Elodie Villalobos, though Marcus remembers him and leaves flowers at the empty lot. Sometimes, wind through the rubble carries three full verses, ending in peace. Beat: elegiac resolution—truth served, memory both erased and preserved.
